title: Writing results for planners, finance and auditors

blocks.text: 9.3.4 Writing Results for Planners, Finance and Auditors

The 2029 budget cut of lesson 9.3.3 has been run, diffed and priced. Now it has to be *written up*, and for three readers at once. The planning team wants to know which projects moved and why, so it can tell the fleet teams. Finance wants the money by year and what the cut costs in value. The internal auditor, who will one day stand behind this plan in a rate case, wants to know exactly what was run, on which inputs, and whether anyone can check it. Lesson 7.1.4 set out what each group needs from an optimizer; this lesson writes one result three ways and states the rules that make each version trustworthy.

The rule that holds them together comes first: **every number in every version comes from data the program produced**, collected once in a record. A memo typed by hand from a screen of output is how a plan's NPV ends up as $23,068k in one email and $23,086k in another. Printing fewer numbers does not fix that: each reader still needs theirs, and any number copied by hand can be copied wrong.
GridCap is a fictional utility, generated for this course; no number in it describes a real one.
The Model

The result is the cut scenario of lesson 9.3.3: the model of lesson 9.3.2 with $`B_{2029} = 6{,}000`$, solved to a relative gap of 0, compared with the base scenario ($`B_{2029} = 8{,}760`$), and with each changed decision priced by a forced re-solve of the cut scenario (lesson 9.3.2's $`\Delta_{\text{in}}`$, $`\Delta_{\text{out}}`$ and $`\Delta_{\text{at}}`$).

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years, 2027 to 2031; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years project $`i`$ may use; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$; $`F^{+}`$ and $`F^{-}`$ the projects forced in and out (empty in both scenarios, except in a pricing re-solve).
**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$, with $`\text{started}(i) = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t}`$ and $`\text{by}(i, t) = \sum_{s \in T_i,\, s \le t} x_{i,s}`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus (M \cup F^{+} \cup F^{-}) && \text{(once}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in F^{+} \setminus M && \text{(in}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 0 && \forall i \in F^{-} && \text{(out}_i) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in g} \text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\text{by}(c, t) &\le \text{by}(p(c),\, t - L_c) && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}
One Record per Run, and Every Text Is Written From It

`record.make_record` solves the scenario and the one it was copied from, diffs them, prices every changed decision with a forced re-solve, checks the plan, reruns it, and returns one dictionary. Its last lines show what goes in:

return {
        "scenario": scenario.name, "parent": parent.name,
        "snapshot": scenario.snapshot(portfolio), "parent_snapshot": parent.snapshot(portfolio),
        "inputs_changed": input_changes(parent.inputs(portfolio), scenario.inputs(portfolio)),
        "software": {"ortools": ortools.__version__, **SETTINGS},
        "status": run.status, "npv": run.npv, "bound": run.result.best_objective_bound(),
        "parent_npv": before.npv, "funded": len(run.plan), "plan": run.plan,
        "selected": d.selected, "deferred": d.deferred, "shifted": d.shifted, "reasons": reasons,
        "budget": {y: scenario.budget.get(y, portfolio.budget[y]) for y in portfolio.years},
        "spend": real_spend(portfolio, run.plan), "parent_spend": real_spend(portfolio, before.plan),
        "checks": verify(portfolio, scenario, run.plan),
        "rerun_same_plan": again.plan == run.plan,
    }
`three_readers.py` builds the record for the cut and prints some of its fields, as JSON:
Three properties make the record the right thing to write from.

items: **It is data, not text.** A reason is stored as facts (`left: 310, needs: 1510`), not as a sentence, so each reader's version can word it its own way and none can change the numbers.
**It is complete.** Each writer reads the record and nothing else: no writer solves, queries the model or looks at a screen. If a version needs a number, the number goes into the record first.

**It can be kept.** JSON goes into a file or a database beside the scenario's snapshot (lesson 12.4.3 designs result schemas, 12.1.4 stores them), so the texts can be written again, or checked, years later.

blocks.text: Note `bound`: MathOpt's `best_objective_bound()`, the solver's proven limit on how good any plan could be. Equal to the NPV, as here, it says the plan is proven optimal; finance and the auditor both read it.
Planners Read Projects, What Changed and the Rule Behind Each

A planner acts project by project, so that version is a list of projects: what happens to each, in words about the rules, and what it would cost to undo. It is lesson 9.3.3's diff with lesson 9.3.2's reasons attached. The rule facts are turned into words by one small function, so that every reason reads the same way:

PLANNERS
Scenario cut-2029 funds 26 projects. Against base:
- P001 leaves the plan (its alternative P002 is in the plan; no room in the budget of 2028 (50 left, needs 1,320), 2029 (310 left, needs 1,320), 2030 (0 left, needs 1,320), 2031 (50 left, needs 1,320)). Putting it back costs $45k.
- P005 leaves the plan (no room in the budget of 2029 (310 left, needs 1,510), 2030 (0 left, needs 1,510)). Putting it back costs $57k.
- P016 leaves the plan (no room in the budget of 2030 (0 left, needs 310), 2031 (50 left, needs 950)). Putting it back costs $68k.
- P002 joins the plan. Taking it out again costs $45k.
- P037 joins the plan. Taking it out again costs $57k.
- P008 starts 2029 instead of 2031 (earlier). Holding it at 2031 costs $68k.
- P011 starts 2029 instead of 2031 (earlier). Holding it at 2031 costs $68k.
- P012 starts 2030 instead of 2031 (earlier). Holding it at 2031 costs $43k.
- P021 starts 2028 instead of 2029 (earlier). Holding it at 2029 costs $68k.
- P025 starts 2029 instead of 2028 (later). Holding it at 2028 costs $45k.
- P035 starts 2028 instead of 2027 (later). Holding it at 2027 costs $3k.
Changes that cost under $50k to reverse are close calls: P001, P002, P012, P025, P035.
What makes this version work for planners:

items: **Every line is about a project**, in the order a planner acts: what leaves, what joins, what moves. Row names such as `budget_2030` are translated ("no room in the budget of 2030"); the facts behind them stay in the record for anyone who asks.

**Every change has a reason and a price.** P001 is out because its repair option P002 took its place and no year has $1,320k free; putting it back costs $45k. The price is computed in the *cut* scenario, the one the planner is looking at, so it differs from lesson 9.3.2's base-scenario prices.

**It says where the plan is fragile.** Five changes cost under $50k to undo. The threshold is a choice the planning team makes once and writes down (here about 0.2% of the plan's NPV); the program only applies it. Those five are where a planner's local knowledge should win, and where a small change of inputs could flip the plan (lesson 9.3.3's near ties).

blocks.text: Finance Reads Money by Year, the Change in Value, and Whether It Is Proven
Finance reads the same record through money: what is spent each year against what was authorized, what the change does to value, and whether the value is a proven optimum or a solver's best effort.

gap = abs(r["bound"] - r["npv"])
    lines.append(f"NPV ${r['npv']:,.0f}k, {r['npv'] - r['parent_npv']:+,.0f}k against {r['parent']} "
                 f"(${r['parent_npv']:,.0f}k); solver status {r['status']}, gap to its bound ${gap:,.0f}k.")

2028   8,120   8,070        50       +100
2029   6,000   5,690       310     -2,940

NPV $23,086k, -1,174k against base ($24,260k); solver status OPTIMAL, gap to its bound $0k.
Spend over the plan falls $2,830k; NPV lost per $k of spend removed: 0.415 (an average over this one change, not a marginal value).
What makes this version work for finance:

items: **Spend by year, against the authorized budget, and against the plan it replaces.** A five-year total hides a year that breaks; here 2030 is spent to the dollar, which finance will want to know before anyone adds to it.
**The spend is summed from the cost profiles**, not read from the model's rows (`real_spend`, lesson 6.4.2), so the table reconciles with the projects' own budgets.

**Value with its proof.** NPV, its change, the solver's status and the gap to the bound. An NPV from a run that stopped early is a lower limit on what the inputs allow (lesson 3.4.1); finance must never read it as the best plan without the gap beside it.

**A ratio labelled for what it is.** Cutting $2,760k of 2029 budget removes $2,830k of spend over the plan and $1,174k of NPV, 0.415 per $k of spend removed. That is an average over one discrete change. It is *not* the value of the next dollar, which on a MILP is a step function; lessons 9.2.3 and 9.2.4 build that curve. The text says so in its own words, so nobody multiplies 0.415 by a different cut.

Auditors Read Inputs, Settings and Checks They Can Repeat Without the Model

An auditor does not need the plan explained; the auditor needs to be able to *repeat* and *check* it. That version lists what was run, on what, with what, and the result of checks that do not trust the model. The checks are the heart of it:

def verify(portfolio: Portfolio, scenario: Scenario, plan: dict[str, int]) -> list[tuple[str, bool]]:
    """Check the plan against every rule from the data alone: no model, no solver."""

("at most one option per alternative group", all(n <= 1 for n in groups.values())),
        ("every funded child starts its lag after its parent",
         all(by_id[p].parent in plan and t >= plan[by_id[p].parent] + by_id[p].parent_lag
             for p, t in plan.items() if by_id[p].parent)),
        ("each year's spend is within its budget", all(spend[y] <= budget[y] for y in portfolio.years)),

AUDITORS

What makes this version work for an auditor:

items: **Full identifiers.** The whole snapshot hash, not the 12 characters a screen shows, and the parent's, so the auditor can match the inputs to a stored scenario (lesson 7.1.3) and see that only the 2029 budget changed.
**The software and settings.** OR-Tools' version, the solver and the gap tolerance. A rerun on different software is a different experiment (lessons 10.2.2 and 10.2.4).

**Checks that do not trust the model.** `verify` reads the portfolio's data and the plan, and nothing the model built. If a row had been written wrongly, the model would have kept the wrong rule and its own slacks would agree with it; the check, written separately from the data, would not. That is lesson 7.1.4's worksheet habit applied to one run. The module's tests show that it catches a plan with both P001 and P002 funded.
**The rerun, reported as evidence.** "Same plan: True" is what one rerun on one machine showed. It is not a guarantee, and the version says what was done rather than "the result is reproducible".

blocks.text: <!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **One record per run, and every text is written from it.** The record holds inputs, snapshot, status, bound, plan, diff, priced reasons, spend and checks, as data; the writers read only the record.
**Planners read projects, what changed and the rule behind each.** One line per project, the rule in words, the price of undoing it, and the close calls.
**Finance reads money by year, the change in value, and whether it is proven.** Spend against budget and against the previous plan, NPV with its gap, and averages labelled as averages.
**Auditors read inputs, settings and checks they can repeat without the model.** Full snapshots, software and settings, rule checks from the data, and a rerun stated as evidence.

blocks.text: **Further reading:** the OR-Tools [MathOpt overview](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (its detailed termination reasons, which the record keeps as `status`); [MathOpt `result.py` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/result.py) (the docstrings of `objective_value`, which points to the primal bound, and `best_objective_bound`, equal to the dual bound: the two numbers finance's line compares); the OR-Tools MathOpt sample [`integer_programming.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/integer_programming.py) (it refuses to read values unless the termination is optimal or feasible, the first thing any of the three versions depends on); the [Gurobi reference for linear constraint attributes](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/reference/attributes/constraintlinear.html) (slack reported per row of the current solution, the kind of fact a record stores). The CIPT job (lesson 9.3.1) names planners, finance partners and regulators as the people who rely on the results, and asks for outputs that explain them.
Challenges

items: Add a line to the finance version that names the year with the least headroom. Which field of the record does it need, and is it already there?
Write a fourth version, for the board: three sentences, no table. Which record fields does it use?
Break `verify` on purpose: change its budget check to compare with the *base* budgets. Predict which line of the auditors' version changes for the cut scenario.

blocks.text: Design Note: Templates in Code, Not Prose in Code

The three writers here are small Python functions that format strings. That is enough to show the rules, and it keeps every number tied to the record. A real service would keep the record as a typed schema (lesson 12.4.3) and the wording in templates that people outside the team can edit, because the people who know how finance wants a sentence phrased are not the people who write the solver. Whatever the tooling, the rule stands: wording may change freely, numbers may come only from the record.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.
